tool.name: Bash
tool.tagline: The standard Unix shell for running commands and writing scripts
tool.description: Bash (the Bourne Again SHell) is the command interpreter on most Linux systems and the language of countless build, deploy and automation scripts. It glues programs together with pipes, redirection and variables, and adds loops, functions and arrays for real scripting. Knowing it well makes you faster at the terminal and lets you read and write the scripts that run CI pipelines, containers and servers.

concepts.name: The shell and running commands
concepts.summary: What a shell is, how a command line is split into a command and arguments, and how to find help.
concepts.why: Every other shell skill builds on reading and typing command lines correctly.
concepts.body:
A **shell** is a program that reads command lines, finds the programs they name and runs them. Bash is the default shell on most Linux distributions and the usual language of `.sh` scripts. When you open a terminal you get a prompt; you type a line and press Enter.

Bash splits the line into words on spaces and tabs. The first word is the command, the rest are its **arguments**. By convention short options look like `-l`, long ones like `--all`, and short ones can often be bundled (`ls -la`). Separate several commands on one line with `;`, and start a comment with `#`.

A command can be one of several kinds, and `type` tells you which:

- a **builtin** such as `cd` or `echo`, implemented inside bash itself,
- an **alias** or **function** you or your config defined,
- an **external program** found by searching the directories in `$PATH`.

For help, use `help name` for builtins and `man name` (or `name --help`) for programs. Interactive conveniences pay off quickly: Tab completes commands and file names, Up/Down walk through history, Ctrl-R searches it, Ctrl-C interrupts the running command and Ctrl-L clears the screen.
concepts.code:
echo hello   world          # hello world   (extra spaces just separate words)
type cd                     # cd is a shell builtin
type ls                     # ls is /usr/bin/ls   (or an alias, interactively)
echo "$BASH_VERSION"        # 5.2.21(1)-release
help echo | head -n 1       # echo: echo [-neE] [arg ...]
ls -la /tmp | head -n 2     # bundled short options
date; pwd                   # two commands on one line
# everything after # is a comment
takeaways: Command line = command word + arguments, split on whitespace
type tells you if a name is a builtin, alias, function or program
help for builtins, man or --help for programs
pitfalls: Expecting several spaces between arguments to be kept: unquoted whitespace only separates words.

quiz.q: Which command tells you whether cd is a builtin or a program on disk?
quiz.explain: type knows about builtins, aliases and functions; which only searches PATH.

quiz.q: How many arguments does `ls -l  /tmp   /var` pass to ls?
quiz.explain: The words after the command are -l, /tmp and /var; extra spaces only separate words.

concepts.name: Variables
concepts.summary: Create, read and remove shell variables, and learn the special parameters bash sets for you.
concepts.why: Variables hold paths, names and settings in every script and are the first thing you expand.
concepts.body:
Assign with `name=value` and **no spaces around `=`**: `name = value` would run a command called `name`. Read a variable with `$name`, or `${name}` when the name must be separated from following text, as in `${name}_backup`.

Every bash variable is a string unless you declare otherwise; `count=5` stores the text `5`, and arithmetic happens only inside `$(( ))`. Referencing a variable that was never set silently gives an empty string, which is why typos are dangerous (strict mode, later, fixes that). Remove a variable with `unset name` and protect one with `readonly NAME=value`; assigning to a read-only variable is an error that aborts a non-interactive script.

Bash maintains several **special parameters**:

- `$?` exit status of the last command, `$$` PID of the shell,
- `$0` script name, `$1`, `$2`... positional arguments, `$#` how many,
- `$RANDOM` a random integer, `$PWD` the current directory, `$HOME` your home.

Convention: lower-case names for your own script variables and UPPER_CASE for environment variables and constants, so you never clobber `PATH` or `HOME` by accident. Values with spaces must be quoted when assigned: `title="My report"`.
takeaways: name=value with no spaces; read it with "$name" or "${name}"
Unset variables expand to an empty string, silently
Use lower-case names for script variables, UPPER_CASE for environment ones
pitfalls: Writing `x = 5`: bash runs a command named x with arguments = and 5.

quiz.q: What does `greeting = hi` do in bash?
options: Runs a command named greeting with two arguments
quiz.explain: Spaces make it a normal command line: the command is greeting, the arguments are = and hi.

quiz.q: After `v=10`, what does `echo "$v1"` print?
quiz.explain: Bash looks for a variable named v1, which is unset and expands to nothing; write ${v}1 for 101.

concepts.name: Quoting: single, double and none
concepts.summary: How single quotes, double quotes and backslashes control which characters bash interprets.
concepts.why: Unquoted variables are the single most common source of shell bugs, from broken file names to deleted data.
concepts.body:
After bash expands an **unquoted** variable, it does two more things to the result: **word splitting** (cutting it at spaces, tabs and newlines) and **globbing** (treating `*`, `?` and `[...]` as file-name patterns). That is why `rm $file` with `file="my report.txt"` tries to delete two files, `my` and `report.txt`.

Quotes switch that off:

- **Double quotes** `"..."` keep the text as one word but still expand `$var`, `$(command)` and `$((math))`. Use them around nearly every expansion: `"$file"`, `"$@"`.
- **Single quotes** `'...'` are completely literal; nothing inside is expanded, and a single quote cannot appear inside them.
- A **backslash** escapes the next character: `echo \$HOME` prints `$HOME`.
- `$'...'` (ANSI-C quoting) understands escapes like `\n` and `\t`.

Quotes can be mixed in one word: `'It'\''s'` or `"$name"'s file'`. They are removed before the command sees its arguments, so `echo "a"b'c'` receives the single argument `abc`.

The rule of thumb is simple: **quote every expansion unless you deliberately want splitting or globbing**. Inside `[[ ]]` and on the right of a plain assignment, bash does not split, but quoting there is harmless too.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)"
file="my report.txt"
touch "$file"
ls $file          # ls: cannot access 'my' ... and 'report.txt' (two words!)
ls "$file"        # my report.txt
echo '$HOME is literal'     # $HOME is literal
echo "Home is $HOME"        # Home is /home/you
echo \$HOME                 # $HOME
echo $'col1\tcol2'          # col1    col2
star="*"
echo $star        # my report.txt   (the * was globbed!)
echo "$star"      # *
echo "a"b'c'      # abc  (quotes are removed, pieces join)
takeaways: Unquoted expansions are split on whitespace and globbed
Double quotes: one word, variables still expand; single quotes: fully literal
Default to "$var" and "$@" everywhere
pitfalls: Writing for f in $(ls) or rm $dir/* with unquoted variables that can contain spaces or be empty.

quiz.q: With `f="a b"`, how many arguments does `touch $f` pass to touch?
quiz.explain: The unquoted expansion is word-split into a and b.

quiz.q: What does `echo '$USER'` print?
quiz.explain: Single quotes prevent all expansion, and the quotes themselves are removed.

concepts.name: Exit status, && and ||
concepts.summary: Every command returns a number: 0 means success. Chain commands on success or failure with && and ||.
concepts.why: Exit statuses are how shell scripts make decisions and detect errors.
concepts.body:
When a command finishes it returns an **exit status**, an integer 0 to 255. **Zero means success**, anything else means failure, and programs document what their non-zero codes mean: `grep` returns 1 for "no match" and 2 for a real error. The status of the last command is in `$?`; read it immediately, because the next command overwrites it.

Bash lets you chain on that status:

- `a && b` runs `b` only if `a` succeeded,
- `a || b` runs `b` only if `a` failed,
- `! a` inverts the status.

So `mkdir -p out && cd out` changes directory only when the directory exists, and `command -v jq || echo "please install jq"` is a one-line dependency check. You can combine them, but `a && b || c` is not a true if/else: `c` also runs when `b` fails.

Your own scripts end with the status of the last command run, or the number passed to `exit`. Use `exit 0` for success and a small non-zero number (often 1, or 2 for usage errors) for failure so callers, cron and CI systems can react. `true` and `false` are commands that simply return 0 and 1.
concepts.code:
grep -q root /etc/passwd
echo $?                       # 0  (found)
grep -q nosuchuser /etc/passwd
echo $?                       # 1  (no match)
ls /nope 2>/dev/null; echo $? # 2  (error)
mkdir -p build && echo "created"     # created
false || echo "fallback ran"         # fallback ran
! true; echo $?               # 1  (! inverts)
true; false; echo $?          # 1  (only the last command counts)
command -v git >/dev/null && echo "git is installed"
takeaways: 0 = success, 1-255 = failure; $? holds the last status
&& runs on success, || on failure, ! inverts
End scripts with a meaningful exit code
pitfalls: Using `a && b || c` as if/else: c also runs when b fails.

quiz.q: What is printed by `false; true; echo $?`?
quiz.explain: $? is the status of the most recent command, true, which returns 0.

quiz.q: In `make && ./app || echo failed`, when is 'failed' printed?
quiz.explain: || reacts to the status of the whole && chain, so a failure of either command triggers it.

concepts.name: Writing and running a script
concepts.summary: Put commands in a file with a shebang, make it executable and read its arguments.
concepts.why: Scripts turn a sequence of commands you keep retyping into a reusable tool.
concepts.body:
A script is a text file of commands. Its first line, the **shebang**, tells the kernel which interpreter to use: `#!/usr/bin/env bash` finds bash on the `PATH` and is the most portable choice. Make the file executable once with `chmod +x script.sh`, then run it as `./script.sh`. The `./` is needed because the current directory is not on `PATH`. Alternatively `bash script.sh` runs it without the execute bit (and ignores the shebang).

Arguments arrive as **positional parameters**:

- `$1`, `$2`, ... the arguments; use `${10}` from the tenth on,
- `$#` the number of arguments, `$0` the name the script was called by,
- `"$@"` all arguments, each kept as a separate word: the right way to pass them on.

`${2:-Hello}` means "the second argument, or Hello if it is missing or empty"; you will see more of these expansions later. A script runs in a **new process**, so `cd` or variables set inside it do not affect your terminal; use `source script.sh` when you actually want that.

Name scripts clearly, keep a usage comment at the top, and exit with a non-zero status on errors.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)"
cat > greet.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# usage: greet.sh NAME [GREETING]
name=$1
greeting=${2:-Hello}
echo "$greeting, $name! ($# args, called as $0)"
EOF
chmod +x greet.sh
./greet.sh Ada              # Hello, Ada! (1 args, called as ./greet.sh)
./greet.sh Bob "Hi there"   # Hi there, Bob! (2 args, called as ./greet.sh)
bash greet.sh Cy            # Hello, Cy! (1 args, called as greet.sh)
takeaways: Start with #!/usr/bin/env bash and chmod +x the file
$1..$9, ${10}, $# and "$@" give you the arguments
A script runs in a child process; source it to affect the current shell
pitfalls: Running `script.sh` without ./ and getting 'command not found' because . is not on PATH.

quiz.q: Inside a script called as `./s.sh a "b c"`, what is $#?
quiz.explain: "b c" is quoted, so it is a single argument; there are two.

quiz.q: A script does `cd /tmp`. Why is your terminal still in the old directory afterwards?
options: The script ran in a separate child process
quiz.explain: Each script gets its own process with its own working directory; use source to run it in the current shell.

concepts.name: if and test conditions
concepts.summary: Branch with if/elif/else using [[ ]] tests on strings, numbers and files, and (( )) for arithmetic.
concepts.why: Checking that files exist, arguments are present or values match is the core of every script.
concepts.body:
`if` runs a command and takes the branch when its exit status is 0. The command is usually a test:

- `[ ... ]` is the classic POSIX `test` command (it is literally a program named `[`), so it needs spaces around brackets and quotes around variables.
- `[[ ... ]]` is a bash keyword: it does not word-split variables, supports `&&` and `||` inside, `==` with glob patterns and `=~` with regular expressions. Prefer it in bash scripts.
- `(( ... ))` evaluates arithmetic and succeeds when the result is non-zero.

Common tests: strings `-z` (empty), `-n` (non-empty), `==`, `!=`; numbers `-eq -ne -lt -le -gt -ge` (or `<` and `>` inside `(( ))`); files `-e` exists, `-f` regular file, `-d` directory, `-r -w -x` permissions, `-s` non-empty.

The syntax is `if cond; then ...; elif cond; then ...; else ...; fi`. Any command works as a condition: `if grep -q error log.txt; then` is idiomatic and faster than capturing output.

Watch out: inside `[[ ]]`, `<` and `>` compare **strings** alphabetically, so `[[ 10 < 9 ]]` is true. Use `-lt` or `(( ))` for numbers. After an `=~` match, captured groups are in the `BASH_REMATCH` array.
concepts.code:
f=/etc/passwd
if [[ -d $f ]]; then
  echo "$f is a directory"
elif [[ -f $f && -r $f ]]; then
  echo "$f is a readable file"     # this branch runs
else
  echo "$f: not found"
fi
name=""
[[ -z $name ]] && echo "name is empty"            # name is empty
n=7
if (( n > 5 )); then echo "big"; fi              # big
if [ "$n" -lt 10 ]; then echo "single digit"; fi # single digit
s="report.csv"
[[ $s == *.csv ]] && echo "CSV file"             # CSV file
[[ $s =~ ^([a-z]+)\. ]] && echo "${BASH_REMATCH[1]}"   # report
[[ 10 < 9 ]] && echo "string comparison!"        # string comparison!
takeaways: if takes the branch when the condition command exits 0
Prefer [[ ]] for strings and files, (( )) for numbers
Any command can be a condition: if grep -q ...; then
pitfalls: Comparing numbers with < or == inside [[ ]], which compares them as strings.

quiz.q: What does `[[ 10 < 9 ]]` return?
quiz.explain: Inside [[ ]], < compares strings lexicographically; use -lt or (( )) for numbers.

quiz.q: Which test is true when $dir names an existing directory?
quiz.explain: -d checks for a directory; -n only checks the string is non-empty.

concepts.name: for and while loops
concepts.summary: Repeat work over lists, files, number ranges and conditions with for, while and until.
concepts.why: Loops let one script process every file, server or line instead of one at a time.
concepts.body:
The **for-in** loop iterates over words: `for x in a b c; do ...; done`. The list is usually a glob (`*.txt`), a quoted array (`"${files[@]}"`) or brace expansion (`{1..10}`, `{a,b,c}`). Iterating over `$(ls)` is a classic mistake: file names with spaces get split; use a glob instead.

If a glob matches nothing, bash leaves the pattern itself as the single word (`*.txt`), so guard with `[[ -e $f ]] || continue`, or enable `shopt -s nullglob` to make it expand to nothing.

The **C-style** loop `for ((i = 0; i < n; i++))` is handy for counters. **while** repeats as long as its condition command succeeds, and **until** repeats until it succeeds, which suits polling: `until curl -fs localhost:8080/health; do sleep 1; done`.

Inside any loop, `break` leaves it and `continue` jumps to the next iteration; both accept a number to affect enclosing loops. A loop is a compound command, so you can redirect or pipe it as a whole: `done > out.txt` writes everything the loop prints into one file, opened once.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)" && touch a.txt b.txt
for fruit in apple "star fruit" kiwi; do
  echo "- $fruit"
done                         # - apple / - star fruit / - kiwi
for f in *.txt; do
  [[ -e $f ]] || continue    # no match would leave the literal '*.txt'
  echo "found $f"
done                         # found a.txt / found b.txt
for ((i = 1; i <= 3; i++)); do printf 'i=%d ' "$i"; done; echo   # i=1 i=2 i=3
for n in {1..5}; do printf '%s ' "$n"; done; echo               # 1 2 3 4 5
count=0
while (( count < 3 )); do
  count=$(( count + 1 ))
done
echo "count=$count"          # count=3
until [[ -f ready ]]; do touch ready; done && echo "ready"      # ready
takeaways: for x in words / glob / "${arr[@]}"; for ((;;)) for counters
while repeats on success, until repeats on failure
Iterate over globs, never over $(ls)
pitfalls: Forgetting that a non-matching glob stays as the literal pattern, so the loop runs once with '*.txt'.

quiz.q: In an empty directory, how many times does `for f in *.log; do echo "$f"; done` print, by default?
quiz.explain: Without nullglob an unmatched glob stays literal, so the loop runs once with the pattern.

quiz.q: Which loop keeps retrying a command until it succeeds?
quiz.explain: until runs the body while the condition fails and stops on the first success.

concepts.name: Redirection: >, >>, 2> and <
concepts.summary: Send a command's output and errors to files, read input from files and silence noise with /dev/null.
concepts.why: Saving output, logging errors and feeding files into commands are everyday shell tasks.
concepts.body:
Every process starts with three open **file descriptors**: 0 standard input, 1 standard output, 2 standard error. By default all three are the terminal. Redirection reconnects them before the command starts:

- `> file` writes stdout to a file, **truncating** it first; `>> file` appends.
- `2> file` sends stderr to a file; `2>> file` appends.
- `2>&1` makes fd 2 point wherever fd 1 currently points; `&> file` is bash shorthand for "both to file".
- `< file` feeds the file to stdin.
- `/dev/null` discards whatever is written to it.

Redirections are processed **left to right**, which makes order matter: `cmd > out.txt 2>&1` sends both streams to the file, while `cmd 2>&1 > out.txt` first points stderr at the terminal (where stdout was at that moment) and only then moves stdout.

Keeping errors on stderr is a convention worth following in your own scripts too: `echo "error: missing file" >&2`. Then a caller can redirect your normal output to a file and still see the errors.

Beware `sort data.txt > data.txt`: the shell truncates the file before sort reads it, leaving it empty. Write to a temporary file and move it, or use `sponge` from moreutils. `set -o noclobber` makes `>` refuse to overwrite existing files.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)"
echo "first" > out.txt        # create or truncate
echo "second" >> out.txt      # append
cat out.txt                   # first / second
ls /nope 2> err.txt           # the error goes to the file
cat err.txt                   # ls: cannot access '/nope': No such file or directory
ls /tmp /nope > all.txt 2>&1  # both streams into the file
ls /tmp /nope &> all.txt      # bash shorthand for the same
wc -l < out.txt               # 2  (stdin from a file: no name printed)
ls /nope 2>/dev/null || echo "quietly failed"   # quietly failed
echo "error: something broke" >&2               # write to stderr
takeaways: fd 0 stdin, 1 stdout, 2 stderr; > truncates, >> appends
cmd > file 2>&1 captures both; order of redirections matters
Send your own error messages to >&2
pitfalls: `sort f > f` empties the file: the shell truncates it before sort reads it.

quiz.q: Which line writes both stdout and stderr of cmd into log.txt?
quiz.explain: Redirections run left to right: first stdout goes to the file, then stderr is pointed at the same place.

quiz.q: What does `wc -l < notes.txt` print compared with `wc -l notes.txt`?
options: Only the count, without the file name
quiz.explain: With < wc reads anonymous stdin and does not know the file name.

concepts.name: Pipelines
concepts.summary: Connect commands with | so each one's output becomes the next one's input.
concepts.why: Pipelines let small tools combine into powerful one-liners for searching, counting and transforming data.
concepts.body:
A **pipeline** `a | b | c` connects the stdout of each command to the stdin of the next. All the commands start at the same time and data streams through them, so pipelines work on files far bigger than memory and the first results appear quickly.

The Unix philosophy is to build pipelines from small tools: `sort`, `uniq -c`, `head`, `tail`, `wc -l`, `cut`, `tr`, `grep`, `awk` and `sed`. A typical pattern: filter lines with grep, extract a field with cut or awk, then `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head` for a top-10 list.

Only stdout goes into the pipe. To include errors, use `2>&1 |` or the bash shorthand `|&`.

The **exit status of a pipeline is the status of its last command**, so `failing-command | tee log.txt` looks successful. Bash keeps every stage's status in the `PIPESTATUS` array, and `set -o pipefail` makes the pipeline fail if any stage fails; most scripts should turn it on.

When an early command stops reading, say `head -n 1` exits, the writer gets a SIGPIPE and stops quietly. That is normal and why `yes | head -n 3` terminates.
concepts.code:
printf '%s\n' banana apple cherry apple | sort | uniq -c
#   2 apple
#   1 banana
#   1 cherry
seq 1 100 | tail -n 3 | awk '{ s += $1 } END { print s }'   # 297
cut -d: -f7 /etc/passwd | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 3
ls /nope 2>&1 | wc -l          # 1  (stderr sent into the pipe)
ls /nope |& wc -l              # 1  (bash shorthand)
false | true; echo $?          # 0  (status of the LAST command)
false | true; echo "${PIPESTATUS[@]}"   # 1 0
yes | head -n 2                # y / y  (yes stops on SIGPIPE)
takeaways: a | b feeds a's stdout into b's stdin; stages run concurrently
Use 2>&1 | or |& to pipe errors too
A pipeline's status is the last command's unless pipefail is set
pitfalls: Assuming `cmd | tee log` fails when cmd fails: without pipefail it reports tee's success.

quiz.q: What is the exit status of `false | true` without pipefail?
options: It depends on the shell options of false
quiz.explain: Without pipefail, a pipeline returns the status of its last command, true.

quiz.q: Why does `yes | head -n 2` finish even though yes never ends on its own?
options: yes gets SIGPIPE when writing to a closed pipe
quiz.explain: After head exits, the pipe's read end is closed and the next write from yes raises SIGPIPE.

concepts.name: Parameter expansion tricks
concepts.summary: Defaults, substrings, prefix/suffix stripping, search-and-replace and case changes, all without external tools.
concepts.why: These expansions replace many calls to sed, basename and dirname and make scripts faster and shorter.
concepts.body:
`${...}` can do much more than read a variable. The forms you will use constantly:

- **Defaults**: `${var:-def}` gives `def` if var is unset or empty; `${var:=def}` also assigns it; `${var:?message}` aborts the script with the message; `${var:+alt}` gives `alt` only when var is set.
- **Remove a prefix/suffix pattern**: `#` removes the shortest matching prefix, `##` the longest; `%` and `%%` do the same at the end. So `${path##*/}` is the base name and `${path%/*}` the directory, `${file%.*}` drops the extension.
- **Replace**: `${var/old/new}` first match, `${var//old/new}` all matches; patterns are globs, not regexes.
- **Length and substrings**: `${#var}` and `${var:offset:length}`; negative offsets need a space: `${var: -3}`.
- **Case** (bash 4+): `${var^}` capitalizes the first letter, `${var^^}` upper-cases all, `${var,,}` lower-cases.

Without the colon (`${var-def}`) the default applies only when var is **unset**, not when it is empty. That distinction matters for optional settings where an empty value is meaningful.

These expansions run inside the shell, so they are much faster in loops than spawning `basename` or `sed` for every item.
concepts.code:
path="/var/log/nginx/access.log.gz"
echo "${path##*/}"        # access.log.gz        (basename)
echo "${path%/*}"         # /var/log/nginx       (dirname)
echo "${path%.gz}"        # /var/log/nginx/access.log
echo "${path#*.}"         # log.gz               (up to the first dot)
echo "${#path}"           # 28
echo "${path/log/LOG}"    # /var/LOG/nginx/access.log.gz
echo "${path//log/LOG}"   # /var/LOG/nginx/access.LOG.gz
echo "${path:5:3}"        # log
echo "${path: -2}"        # gz
unset port
echo "${port:-8080}"      # 8080  (port is still unset)
echo "${port:=3000} $port"     # 3000 3000
name=ada
echo "${name^} ${name^^}" # Ada ADA
# : "${API_KEY:?must be set}"  -> aborts: API_KEY: must be set
takeaways: ${v:-def} default, ${v:=def} assign, ${v:?msg} require
# and ## strip prefixes, % and %% strip suffixes
${v//a/b} replaces with glob patterns; ${#v} is the length
pitfalls: Writing ${var:-3} when you meant the last 3 characters: you need ${var: -3} with a space.

quiz.q: With f=archive.tar.gz, what is ${f%%.*}?
quiz.explain: %% removes the longest suffix matching .*, which starts at the first dot.

quiz.q: What does ${name:-guest} give when name is set to the empty string?
quiz.explain: The colon form treats empty the same as unset; ${name-guest} would give the empty string.

concepts.name: Command substitution and arithmetic
concepts.summary: Capture a command's output with $(...) and do integer math with $(( )) and (( )).
concepts.why: Scripts constantly need dates, counts and computed values from other commands.
concepts.body:
**Command substitution** `$(command)` runs the command and replaces itself with the command's stdout, minus **trailing newlines**. Use it to store results: `today=$(date +%F)`, `n=$(wc -l < file)`. The old backtick form does the same but nests badly; prefer `$( )`, which nests cleanly: `$(dirname "$(readlink -f "$0")")`.

Quote the substitution when using it as an argument, `"$(cmd)"`, or the output will be word-split and globbed like any unquoted expansion. In a plain assignment `x=$(cmd)` no quotes are needed, but they do no harm.

**Arithmetic expansion** `$(( expr ))` evaluates integer math with C-like operators: `+ - * / % **`, comparisons, `&&`, `||`, bit operators and the ternary `?:`. Variables inside need no `$`. Division truncates; bash has **no floating point**, so reach for `awk` or `bc` when you need decimals.

The command form `(( expr ))` evaluates without printing and returns success when the result is non-zero, which makes it ideal for conditions and counters: `(( count++ ))`, `if (( n % 2 == 0 ))`. Note that `(( x++ ))` returns failure when x was 0, which matters under `set -e`; write `x=$(( x + 1 ))` there.

Numbers with a leading zero, like `08`, are read as octal and error out; strip zeros or write `10#$n`.
concepts.code:
today=$(date +%F)
entries=$(ls / | wc -l)
echo "Today is $today; / has $entries entries"
kernel="$(uname -r)"
echo "Running kernel $kernel"
lines=$(printf 'a\nb\n\n\n')   # trailing newlines are stripped
echo "${#lines}"               # 3  ("a", newline, "b")
x=7 y=3
echo $(( x * y + 1 ))          # 22
echo $(( x / y )) $(( x % y )) # 2 1   (integers only)
echo $(( 2 ** 10 ))            # 1024
(( x > y )) && echo "x wins"   # x wins
month=08
echo $(( 10#$month + 1 ))      # 9   (force base 10, avoid octal)
awk 'BEGIN { printf "%.2f\n", 10 / 3 }'   # 3.33  (floats need another tool)
takeaways: $(cmd) captures stdout without trailing newlines; quote it as an argument
$(( )) for integer math, (( )) for arithmetic conditions
No floats in bash: use awk or bc
pitfalls: Leading zeros: $(( 08 + 1 )) fails because 08 is parsed as an invalid octal number.

quiz.q: What does `echo $(( 7 / 2 ))` print?
quiz.explain: Bash arithmetic is integer only and division truncates toward zero.

quiz.q: Why prefer $(...) over backticks?
quiz.explain: Both capture output, but $(...) can be nested without escaping and is easier to read.

concepts.name: Functions
concepts.summary: Define reusable functions with local variables, arguments, return statuses and output.
concepts.why: Functions keep scripts readable and testable instead of one long stream of commands.
concepts.body:
Define a function with `name() { commands; }` and call it like any command: `name arg1 arg2`. Inside, the arguments are `$1`, `$2`, `$#` and `"$@"`, just like a script; `$0` still names the script.

Variables are **global by default**, so a function that sets `i` clobbers the caller's `i`. Declare working variables with `local` (it is dynamically scoped: functions called from yours see them too).

Functions "return" in two ways:

- **Status**: `return N` (0-255), or implicitly the status of the last command. This is for success/failure, so a function like `is_even` can be used directly in `if`.
- **Data**: print it to stdout and capture with `result=$(myfunc)`. Send logs and errors to stderr (`>&2`) so they do not pollute captured output.

Capturing with `$( )` runs the function in a **subshell**, so variable changes inside are lost; if you need to set a caller's variable, use a global or a name reference (`local -n ref=$1`, bash 4.3+).

Define functions before calling them (bash reads scripts top to bottom). A common layout is: settings, functions, then a `main "$@"` call at the very end, which also keeps a half-downloaded script from running partially.
concepts.code:
log() { printf '[%s] %s\n' "$(date +%T)" "$*" >&2; }
max() {
  local a=$1 b=$2            # local: invisible outside the function
  if (( a > b )); then echo "$a"; else echo "$b"; fi
}
is_even() { (( $1 % 2 == 0 )); }    # status of last command = result
set_var() { local -n ref=$1; ref=$2; }   # nameref: write caller's variable
main() {
  log "starting"             # [12:00:00] starting  (on stderr)
  local biggest
  biggest=$(max 4 9)         # data comes back via stdout
  echo "max=$biggest"        # max=9
  if is_even 10; then echo "10 is even"; fi   # 10 is even
  is_even 7 || echo "7 is odd"                # 7 is odd
  set_var color blue; echo "color=$color"     # color=blue
}
main "$@"
takeaways: name() { ...; } with $1, $2, "$@" for arguments
Use local for every working variable
return is a status; output data on stdout and capture with $( )
pitfalls: Using `return "$value"` to return data: it is a 0-255 status code, not a value.

quiz.q: A function sets `count=5` without local. What happens to a global count?
quiz.explain: Variables in bash functions are global unless declared local.

quiz.q: How should a function hand a string result to its caller?
quiz.explain: return only carries a 0-255 status; printing and capturing is the idiomatic way to return data.

concepts.name: Indexed and associative arrays
concepts.summary: Store lists and key/value maps in arrays, loop over them safely and pass them on intact.
concepts.why: Arrays are the only safe way to hold lists of file names or arguments that may contain spaces.
concepts.body:
An **indexed array** is created with `arr=(a "b c" d)` and grows with `arr+=(e)`. Index from 0: `${arr[1]}`. The essential expansions:

- `"${arr[@]}"` every element as a separate word (always quote it),
- `${#arr[@]}` number of elements, `${!arr[@]}` the indices,
- `"${arr[@]:1:2}"` a slice.

Arrays can be **sparse**: after `unset 'arr[0]'` the indices are 1 2 3, so loop over elements or over `${!arr[@]}` rather than assuming 0..n-1.

**Associative arrays** (bash 4+) must be declared: `declare -A port=([http]=80 [https]=443)`. Set with `port[ssh]=22`, read with `${port[ssh]}`, list keys with `"${!port[@]}"`. Key order is not defined, so sort if you need stable output. Test for a key with `[[ -v port[ssh] ]]`.

Arrays shine for building command lines: `args=(--verbose); [[ $dry ]] && args+=(--dry-run); rsync "${args[@]}" src/ dst/` passes each option as exactly one argument, which string concatenation can not do safely.

To read lines of a file or command into an array use `mapfile -t lines < file` (also called `readarray`). Bash arrays are one-dimensional and cannot be exported to child processes.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)"
fruits=(apple "star fruit" kiwi)
fruits+=(mango)
echo "${fruits[1]}"          # star fruit
echo "${#fruits[@]}"         # 4
for f in "${fruits[@]}"; do printf '<%s>' "$f"; done; echo
# <apple><star fruit><kiwi><mango>
echo "${fruits[@]:1:2}"      # star fruit kiwi
unset 'fruits[0]'
echo "${!fruits[@]}"         # 1 2 3  (sparse!)
declare -A port=([http]=80 [https]=443)
port[ssh]=22
echo "${port[https]}"        # 443
[[ -v port[ftp] ]] || echo "no ftp"    # no ftp
for k in "${!port[@]}"; do echo "$k=${port[$k]}"; done   # order not guaranteed
printf 'x\ny\n' > two.txt
mapfile -t lines < two.txt
echo "${#lines[@]} lines, first=${lines[0]}"   # 2 lines, first=x
takeaways: "${arr[@]}" expands each element as one word; always quote it
declare -A for key/value maps; keys come back in no particular order
Build command lines in arrays, then run "${cmd[@]}"
pitfalls: Writing ${arr} or $arr, which gives only the first element.

quiz.q: After `a=(x y z); unset 'a[1]'`, what does ${#a[@]} print?
quiz.explain: Two elements remain (indices 0 and 2); the array is now sparse.

quiz.q: Which expansion keeps 'star fruit' as a single word when passed to a command?
quiz.explain: Quoted [@] expands every element to exactly one word; the others split or join.

concepts.name: case statements and glob patterns
concepts.summary: Match strings against glob patterns with case, and master *, ?, [...] and extended globs.
concepts.why: case is the clean way to dispatch on file types, subcommands and options.
concepts.body:
**Glob patterns** match strings and file names: `*` any run of characters, `?` exactly one character, `[abc]` or `[a-z]` one character from a set, `[!0-9]` one not in the set. When used unquoted as arguments, globs expand to matching file names, sorted; hidden files (starting with `.`) only match if the pattern starts with a dot.

The same patterns drive the **case** statement, which compares one word against a list of patterns and runs the first match:

```bash
case $word in
  pat1|pat2) commands ;;
  *) default ;;
esac
```

`|` separates alternatives, `;;` ends a branch, and `*)` is the catch-all. case is cleaner than a chain of `elif [[ $x == ... ]]` and it is POSIX, so it also works in `sh`.

Useful shell options via `shopt -s`:

- `nullglob`: unmatched globs expand to nothing instead of themselves,
- `globstar`: `**` matches across directories, as in `**/*.py`,
- `dotglob`: include hidden files,
- `extglob`: extended patterns `!(pat)`, `@(a|b)`, `+(pat)`, `*(pat)`, `?(pat)`.

Globs are not regular expressions: `*` alone means "anything", there is no `.` wildcard, and you need `[[ =~ ]]` for real regexes.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)"
for name in app.tgz main.c 2024.log --help notes.md; do
  case $name in
    *.tar.gz|*.tgz) kind="tarball" ;;
    *.[ch])         kind="C source" ;;
    [0-9]*)         kind="starts with a digit" ;;
    -h|--help)      kind="help flag" ;;
    *)              kind="other" ;;
  esac
  echo "$name: $kind"
done
# app.tgz: tarball / main.c: C source / 2024.log: starts with a digit
# --help: help flag / notes.md: other
shopt -s nullglob extglob globstar
mkdir -p src/lib && touch a.log b.log c.txt src/x.py src/lib/y.py
logs=(*.log); echo "${#logs[@]} logs"   # 2 logs
echo !(*.log|src)                       # c.txt
echo **/*.py                            # src/lib/y.py src/x.py
none=(*.zip); echo "${#none[@]}"        # 0  (thanks to nullglob)
takeaways: * any string, ? one char, [a-z] one char from a set
case word in pat|pat) ... ;; esac picks the first matching pattern
shopt -s nullglob, globstar and extglob unlock safer, richer globs
pitfalls: Treating globs as regexes, e.g. expecting `.*` to mean 'anything'.

quiz.q: Which case pattern matches both 'y' and 'yes' but not 'yellow'?
quiz.explain: | lists alternatives; y* would also match yellow and [yes] matches one character.

quiz.q: What does `shopt -s nullglob` change?
quiz.explain: Without it, a glob with no matches is left as the literal pattern.

concepts.name: Reading input: read and here-docs
concepts.summary: Read lines and fields safely with while read, and feed text into commands with here-docs and here-strings.
concepts.why: Processing files line by line and embedding templates are bread-and-butter scripting tasks.
concepts.body:
`read` reads one line from stdin into variables. Always use `read -r` (otherwise backslashes are eaten), and set `IFS` for the field separator: with `IFS=: read -r a b c`, the line is split at colons and the **last variable gets the rest** of the line.

The canonical loop for processing a file line by line is:

```bash
while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < file
```

`IFS=` keeps leading and trailing whitespace, `-r` keeps backslashes, and the redirection after `done` feeds the whole loop. If the last line has no trailing newline, add `|| [[ -n $line ]]` to the condition to still process it. Use `_` as a throwaway variable for fields you skip.

Other useful flags: `-p "prompt"` shows a prompt, `-s` hides typing (passwords), `-t 5` times out, `-a arr` reads words into an array.

A **here-document** passes inline text as stdin: `cat <<EOF ... EOF`. Variables and `$( )` expand inside unless the delimiter is quoted (`<<'EOF'`), which makes it literal: ideal for generating config files or scripts. `<<-EOF` strips leading **tabs** so you can indent the block. A **here-string** `<<< "$var"` feeds a single string, handy for `read` and `bc`.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)"
printf 'alice 30\nbob 25\n' > people.txt
while read -r name age; do
  echo "$name is $age"
done < people.txt                 # alice is 30 / bob is 25
IFS=: read -r user _ uid _ < /etc/passwd
echo "$user has uid $uid"         # root has uid 0
read -r first rest <<< "one two three"
echo "$first | $rest"             # one | two three
who=World
cat <<EOF
Hello $who, today is $(date +%A)
EOF
cat <<'EOF'
No $expansion here
EOF
# read -rsp "Password: " pw       # interactive: hidden input
takeaways: while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < file is the line loop
The last variable of read collects the rest of the line
<<EOF expands variables, <<'EOF' is literal, <<< feeds one string
pitfalls: Piping into `while read` and expecting variables set in the loop to survive; the loop runs in a subshell.

quiz.q: With `IFS=, read -r a b <<< "1,2,3"`, what is b?
quiz.explain: The last variable receives the remainder of the line, including later separators.

quiz.q: How do you stop $HOME from expanding inside a here-document?
quiz.explain: A quoted delimiter makes the whole here-document literal.

concepts.name: Environment variables and startup files
concepts.summary: export, per-command variables, PATH, and which of .bashrc and .bash_profile runs when.
concepts.why: Most 'works in my terminal but not in cron or CI' problems come down to the environment.
concepts.body:
Shell variables live only in the current shell. **Exported** variables form the **environment**, which is copied into every child process, so programs and scripts you start can read them. `export NAME=value` creates and exports in one step; `env` or `printenv` lists the environment. Changes in a child never flow back to the parent.

Prefix a command with assignments to set them **for that command only**: `TZ=UTC date` or `LC_ALL=C sort file`. This is how you pass configuration to tools without polluting your shell.

`PATH` is a colon-separated list of directories searched for commands, in order. Add your own with `export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"` (prepend to take priority). After installing something new, `hash -r` clears bash's remembered locations.

Startup files:

- **Login shells** (SSH sessions, a console login, `bash -l`) read `/etc/profile`, then the first of `~/.bash_profile`, `~/.bash_login`, `~/.profile`.
- **Interactive non-login shells** (most terminal tabs on Linux) read `~/.bashrc`.
- **Scripts** read neither, unless `BASH_ENV` points at a file.

The usual setup: put aliases, prompt and functions in `~/.bashrc`, and make `~/.bash_profile` source it. Cron jobs and systemd services start with a minimal environment, so scripts should set the `PATH` and variables they rely on.
concepts.code:
greeting=hi                                 # shell variable only
bash -c 'echo "child sees: [$greeting]"'    # child sees: []
export greeting
bash -c 'echo "child sees: [$greeting]"'    # child sees: [hi]
MODE=fast bash -c 'echo "mode=$MODE"'       # mode=fast  (set for ONE command)
echo "mode=[${MODE:-}]"                     # mode=[]    (not set in this shell)
echo "$PATH" | tr ':' '\n' | head -n 3      # first directories searched
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"        # prepend your own bin
printenv HOME                               # /home/you
# ~/.bash_profile (login shells) typically contains just:
#   [[ -f ~/.bashrc ]] && . ~/.bashrc
# ~/.bashrc (interactive shells): aliases, prompt, functions
takeaways: export copies a variable into the environment of child processes
VAR=value cmd sets a variable for one command only
Login shells read ~/.bash_profile, interactive ones ~/.bashrc, scripts neither
pitfalls: Putting PATH changes only in ~/.bashrc and wondering why a cron job or IDE does not see them.

quiz.q: A script runs `export DEBUG=1`. Is DEBUG set in the terminal that launched the script afterwards?
options: No, environment flows only from parent to child
Only if the script used sudo
Only until the terminal is resized
quiz.explain: The script is a child process; exported variables go to its children, never back to the parent.

quiz.q: Which file does a new interactive, non-login bash on Linux read?
quiz.explain: Interactive non-login shells read ~/.bashrc; login shells read the profile files.

concepts.name: Safer scripts: set -euo pipefail
concepts.summary: Make scripts stop on errors, unset variables and failed pipeline stages, and know the exceptions.
concepts.why: Without these options a script keeps going after a failure and can do real damage with empty variables.
concepts.body:
By default bash ignores failures and keeps running. Three options, usually written together at the top of a script, change that:

- `set -e` (errexit): exit when a command fails.
- `set -u` (nounset): treat expanding an unset variable as an error, which catches typos like `rm -rf "$buidl_dir/"`.
- `set -o pipefail`: a pipeline fails if any stage fails, not just the last.

`set -e` has deliberate exceptions you must know. It does not trigger for commands in an `if`/`while` condition, for any command in a `&&`/`||` list except the last, or for commands negated with `!`. And the status of a command substitution is lost when it is used in `local x=$(cmd)` or `echo "$(cmd)"`; declare first (`local x`) and assign on its own line.

Commands that legitimately return non-zero need handling: `grep` returns 1 for no match, `diff` for differences. Use `|| true`, or test them in an `if`.

With `-u`, optional parameters need defaults: `"${1:-}"`, `"${DEBUG:-0}"`. Some people also set `IFS=$'\n\t'` so unquoted expansions only split on newlines and tabs. Strict mode is a safety net, not a substitute for checking the errors you can anticipate and printing helpful messages.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)"
cat > strict.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
name=${1:-world}              # -u: optional args need defaults
echo "hello $name"
count=$(grep -c foo /dev/null || true)   # grep exits 1 on no match
echo "count=$count"
if ! mkdir /proc/x 2>/dev/null; then     # failures inside if are fine
  echo "mkdir failed, handled"
fi
echo "$undefined_var"         # -u: the script dies here
echo "never printed"
EOF
bash strict.sh; echo "exit status: $?"
# hello world / count=0 / mkdir failed, handled
# strict.sh: line 10: undefined_var: unbound variable
# exit status: 1
takeaways: set -euo pipefail: stop on errors, unset variables and failed pipe stages
-e is suspended in conditions, && / || lists and after !
Give optional variables defaults with ${var:-}
pitfalls: `local out=$(cmd)` hides cmd's failure from set -e because local itself succeeds.

quiz.q: Under `set -e`, does `if grep -q x file; then ...` abort the script when x is not found?
options: No, commands in an if condition are exempt
quiz.explain: errexit ignores failures of commands whose status is being tested.

quiz.q: What does `set -u` catch?
options: Expanding a variable that was never set
quiz.explain: nounset makes expanding an unset variable an error instead of an empty string.

concepts.name: trap: cleanup and signals
concepts.summary: Run cleanup code on exit, errors and signals so temporary files and locks never leak.
concepts.why: Real scripts create temp files, lock files and background processes that must be cleaned up even on failure.
concepts.body:
`trap 'commands' SIGNALS` registers code to run when the shell receives a signal or reaches a special event. The most useful is the **EXIT** pseudo-signal, which fires whenever the script ends: normally, through `exit N`, or because `set -e` aborted it. A single EXIT trap is the bash equivalent of `finally`.

The standard pattern: create resources with `mktemp`, then immediately register the trap.

- Put cleanup in a function and register it with `trap cleanup EXIT`.
- Read `$?` as the first thing in the function to know whether the script failed.
- Use `rm -rf -- "$tmpdir"`; the `--` guards against names starting with a dash.

Other events: `INT` (Ctrl-C), `TERM` (polite kill from systemd, Docker or `kill`), `HUP` (terminal closed), and the bash pseudo-signals `ERR` (a command failed) and `DEBUG` (before every command). By convention a script interrupted by a signal exits with 128 + the signal number, so 130 after Ctrl-C.

`trap - INT` restores the default and `trap '' INT` ignores the signal. `trap -p` shows current traps. **SIGKILL** (9) can never be trapped, so no cleanup runs after `kill -9`; design temp files to be harmless if left behind. Traps are not inherited by subshells in the same way, so set them in the process that owns the resources.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)"
cat > job.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
tmpdir=$(mktemp -d)
cleanup() {
  local status=$?
  rm -rf -- "$tmpdir"
  echo "cleaned up (exit status $status)" >&2
}
trap cleanup EXIT              # normal exit, error, or exit N
trap 'echo "interrupted" >&2; exit 130' INT TERM
echo "working in $tmpdir"
touch "$tmpdir/data"
false                          # set -e aborts here...
echo "not reached"
EOF
bash job.sh
# working in /tmp/tmp.XXXX
# cleaned up (exit status 1)
takeaways: trap cleanup EXIT runs on every exit path: the shell's finally
Trap INT and TERM to exit cleanly with 128 + signal
SIGKILL cannot be trapped
pitfalls: Registering the trap after creating several resources, so an early failure leaks the first ones.

quiz.q: Which trap runs both on a normal end and when set -e aborts the script?
quiz.explain: EXIT fires on every way the shell exits; ERR only on failures, INT only on Ctrl-C.

quiz.q: A process gets `kill -9`. What happens to its EXIT trap?
options: It runs only if set -e is on
quiz.explain: SIGKILL ends the process immediately; nothing in the process gets to run.

concepts.name: Parsing options with getopts
concepts.summary: Accept -v, -o FILE and bundled flags properly with the getopts builtin and a usage message.
concepts.why: Command-line tools that behave like real Unix commands are easier to use and to call from other scripts.
concepts.body:
`getopts optstring var` parses short options one at a time in a `while` loop. Each letter in the optstring is an accepted option; a letter followed by `:` takes a value, which arrives in `$OPTARG`. A leading `:` switches to silent error mode, where you handle problems yourself: an unknown option sets `var` to `?` and a missing value sets it to `:`, with the offending letter in `$OPTARG`.

getopts handles bundling (`-vf`), attached values (`-ofile`) and stops at the first non-option or at `--`. After the loop, `shift $((OPTIND - 1))` removes the parsed options so `"$@"` holds only the operands (files, names...).

Good habits for script interfaces:

- a `usage` function that prints to stderr and exits with status 2,
- defaults set before the loop,
- validate operands after shifting (`(( $# > 0 )) || usage`),
- support `-h` for help.

getopts is a bash builtin and POSIX, so it is portable, but it only understands **short** options. For `--long-options`, either parse manually with a `while (( $# )); do case $1 in ...` loop plus `shift`, or use the util-linux `getopt` program (note: no s), which is available on Linux but differs on macOS.
takeaways: Letters in the optstring are options; a trailing : means it takes a value in $OPTARG
shift $((OPTIND - 1)) leaves only the operands in "$@"
getopts is short-options only; parse --long options manually
pitfalls: Forgetting the shift after the loop, so the options are processed again as file names.

quiz.q: In the optstring 'ab:c', which option takes an argument?
quiz.explain: The colon after b marks it as requiring a value.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of `shift $((OPTIND - 1))` after a getopts loop?
options: Removes the parsed options so $@ holds the operands
Resets getopts for the next call
quiz.explain: OPTIND points at the first unparsed argument; shifting drops everything before it.

concepts.name: Subshells, grouping and process substitution
concepts.summary: Know when code runs in a subshell, group commands with { } and ( ), and treat command output as a file with <( ).
concepts.why: Lost variable updates and puzzling cd behaviour are almost always subshell effects.
concepts.body:
A **subshell** is a forked copy of the current shell. It inherits all variables (exported or not), but nothing it changes, not variables, `cd`, `set` options or traps, makes it back to the parent. Bash creates subshells for:

- `( commands )` explicit grouping,
- `$( command substitution )`,
- each part of a pipeline (all of them by default),
- background jobs `cmd &`.

`{ commands; }` groups **without** a subshell: same process, so changes persist. Use it to redirect several commands at once: `{ date; uname -a; } > info.txt`. Note the required spaces and the final `;`. Use `( )` when you want isolation, such as `(cd build && make)` to change directory temporarily.

The classic trap is `cmd | while read -r line; do count=$((count+1)); done`: the loop runs in a subshell and `count` is unchanged afterwards. Fix it by redirecting instead of piping, using **process substitution**: `done < <(cmd)`.

Process substitution `<(cmd)` runs `cmd` and gives you a file name (like `/dev/fd/63`) connected to its output; `>(cmd)` gives a file name that feeds `cmd`'s input. It lets you pass command output to programs that insist on file arguments: `diff <(sort a) <(sort b)`, or `tee >(gzip > log.gz)`.
concepts.code:
(cd /tmp && pwd)                # /tmp   -- subshell: the cd does not leak
pwd                             # unchanged
{ echo one; echo two; } > /tmp/both.txt   # group, same shell, one redirect
count=0
printf 'a\nb\n' | while read -r _; do count=$((count + 1)); done
echo "pipe: $count"             # pipe: 0     (loop ran in a subshell)
count=0
while read -r _; do count=$((count + 1)); done < <(printf 'a\nb\n')
echo "procsub: $count"          # procsub: 2
diff <(printf '1\n2\n3\n') <(printf '1\n3\n')
# 2d1
# < 2
echo <(true)                    # /dev/fd/63  (it is a file name)
x=1; (x=2); echo "x=$x"         # x=1
takeaways: ( ) and pipeline stages run in subshells; their changes are lost
{ ...; } groups in the current shell
<(cmd) turns output into a readable file name; use done < <(cmd)
pitfalls: Incrementing a counter inside `cmd | while read` and reading it after the loop.

quiz.q: Why does `echo hi | read -r v; echo "$v"` print an empty line in bash by default?
options: read ran in a subshell of the pipeline
quiz.explain: Each pipeline stage runs in a subshell, so v is set only there.

quiz.q: Which grouping runs commands in the current shell?
quiz.explain: Braces group without forking; parentheses, $( ) and pipes create subshells.

concepts.name: Background jobs, wait and parallelism
concepts.summary: Run commands in the background with &, wait for them, check their status and parallelise with xargs -P.
concepts.why: Running independent tasks concurrently can turn a ten-minute script into a one-minute one.
concepts.body:
Ending a command with `&` starts it in the **background**: the shell continues immediately and stores the job's PID in `$!`. `wait` blocks until all background children finish; `wait "$pid"` waits for one and returns **its exit status**, which is how you detect failures of parallel tasks. Bash 5.1 added `wait -n -p var` to wait for whichever job finishes next and report its PID.

In an interactive shell, **job control** manages jobs: `jobs` lists them, Ctrl-Z suspends the foreground job, `bg` resumes it in the background and `fg %1` brings job 1 back. Background jobs die with the terminal unless started with `nohup` or detached with `disown`; for anything long-running, prefer a proper service manager, tmux or screen.

For many small tasks, do not start thousands of `&` jobs at once. Limit concurrency:

- `xargs -P 4 -n 1 cmd` runs up to four commands at a time from input lines (use `-0` with `find -print0` for safe file names),
- GNU `parallel` offers more control,
- or count running jobs and call `wait -n` before starting another.

Output from parallel jobs interleaves unpredictably; write each job's output to its own file, or prefix lines. Remember each background job runs in a subshell, so it cannot set variables in the parent.
concepts.code:
sleep 0.2 & pid1=$!
(sleep 0.1; exit 3) & pid2=$!
wait "$pid2"; echo "job 2 status: $?"   # job 2 status: 3
wait "$pid1"; echo "job 1 status: $?"   # job 1 status: 0
work() { sleep "0.$(( RANDOM % 3 ))"; echo "done $1"; }
for item in a b c; do work "$item" & done
wait                                    # all three done, order varies
printf '%s\n' 1 2 3 4 5 6 |
  xargs -P 3 -I{} sh -c 'sleep 0.1; echo "item {}"'   # 3 at a time
max=2
for n in 1 2 3 4; do
  while (( $(jobs -rp | wc -l) >= max )); do wait -n; done
  work "job$n" &
done
wait
takeaways: cmd & runs in the background; $! is its PID
wait "$pid" returns that job's exit status
Cap concurrency with xargs -P or wait -n
pitfalls: Starting jobs with & and never calling wait, so the script exits before they finish or their failures go unnoticed.

quiz.q: How do you learn whether a background job failed?
quiz.explain: After cmd &, $? is 0 immediately; wait returns the job's real exit status.

quiz.q: What does `xargs -P 4` do?
options: Runs up to 4 commands in parallel
quiz.explain: -P sets the maximum number of processes run at once; -n sets arguments per command.

concepts.name: Debugging and ShellCheck
concepts.summary: Trace scripts with set -x and a better PS4, check syntax with bash -n and catch bugs early with ShellCheck.
concepts.why: Shell bugs are often silent; tracing and static analysis find them in minutes.
concepts.body:
Bash has built-in tools for seeing what a script really does:

- `bash -n script.sh` parses the script without running anything: a quick syntax check.
- `bash -x script.sh`, or `set -x` inside the script, prints every command after expansion, prefixed with `+`. Turn it off again with `set +x` to trace just one section.
- Customise the prefix with `PS4`: `PS4='+ ${BASH_SOURCE}:${LINENO}:${FUNCNAME[0]:-main}: '` adds file, line and function to each traced line. Use single quotes so it expands at trace time.
- `trap '...' ERR` can report the failing command (`$BASH_COMMAND`) and line (`$LINENO`).
- `set -o functrace` and `set -o errtrace` make DEBUG and ERR traps apply inside functions.

**ShellCheck** is a static analyser that knows hundreds of shell pitfalls: unquoted variables (SC2086), `for f in $(ls)`, useless `cat`, `cd` without error handling, unreachable code, variables used but never assigned, and bashisms in `#!/bin/sh` scripts. Every warning has an ID with a wiki page explaining it. Run it in your editor and in CI; disable a specific check on one line with a `# shellcheck disable=SC2086` comment when you are sure.

For harder problems: print values to stderr with `declare -p var`, and reproduce the issue in a small test script before touching the real one.
concepts.code:
bash -n deploy.sh              # syntax check only, runs nothing
bash -x deploy.sh arg1         # trace every command
# inside a script:
PS4='+ ${BASH_SOURCE}:${LINENO}: '
set -x
total=$(( 2 + 3 ))
# + deploy.sh:6: total=5
set +x
trap 'echo "error at line $LINENO: $BASH_COMMAND" >&2' ERR
declare -p total >&2           # declare -- total="5"
shellcheck deploy.sh
# In deploy.sh line 3:
# rm -rf $dir/*
#        ^--^ SC2086 (info): Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting.
takeaways: bash -n checks syntax, set -x traces execution
A PS4 with ${LINENO} makes traces readable
Run ShellCheck on every script, in the editor and in CI
pitfalls: Leaving `set -x` on in a script that handles secrets: they are printed in the trace.

quiz.q: What does `bash -n script.sh` do?
options: Runs the script without a shebang
Parses it for syntax errors without executing
Runs it in a new namespace
quiz.explain: -n (noexec) reads and parses commands but does not run them.

quiz.q: Why should PS4 be set with single quotes?
options: Double quotes are not allowed in PS4
So $LINENO expands each time a line is traced, not once at assignment
quiz.explain: With double quotes, LINENO would be expanded once when PS4 is assigned.

concepts.name: The order of expansions and word splitting
concepts.summary: The exact sequence bash applies to every command line, and how IFS, $@ and $* really behave.
concepts.why: Predicting expansion order explains nearly every 'why did bash do that' surprise.
concepts.body:
Bash processes each command line in a fixed order:

- **Brace expansion**: `{a,b}`, `{1..5}`,
- **tilde expansion**: `~`, `~user`,
- **parameter and variable expansion**, **arithmetic expansion**, **command substitution** and **process substitution**, left to right,
- **word splitting** of the unquoted results of those expansions,
- **pathname expansion** (globbing),
- **quote removal**.

Consequences: `{1..$n}` does not work because braces are expanded before variables. Word splitting only applies to the results of expansions, never to literal text, and quoted results are exempt. File names produced by globbing are never split again, so `for f in *` is safe even with spaces.

Splitting uses **IFS** (default space, tab, newline). Whitespace characters in IFS are trimmed and runs of them collapse; other characters such as `,` or `:` delimit exactly, so empty fields are kept. An empty IFS disables splitting entirely; unset IFS behaves like the default.

`"$@"` expands to each positional parameter as a separate word; `"$*"` joins them into one word using the first character of IFS; unquoted `$@` and `$*` are both split and globbed. The same rules apply to `"${arr[@]}"` versus `"${arr[*]}"`. When building a CSV line, `(IFS=,; echo "$*")` is a neat idiom.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)"
n=3
echo {1..$n}            # {1..3}   braces ran before $n was expanded
echo $(seq 1 "$n")      # 1 2 3
IFS=, read -ra parts <<< "a,b,,c"
echo "${#parts[@]}"     # 4  (non-whitespace IFS keeps the empty field)
data="x  y   z"
set -- $data; echo $#   # 3  (whitespace runs collapse)
IFS=: ; set -- $data; echo $#    # 1  (no colon, one word)
unset IFS
touch a.sh b.sh
pat='*.sh'
echo $pat               # a.sh b.sh  (globbing after expansion)
echo "$pat"             # *.sh
show() { printf '[%s]' "$@"; echo; }
set -- "a b" c
show "$@"               # [a b][c]
show "$*"               # [a b c]
show $*                 # [a][b][c]
(IFS=,; echo "$*")      # a b,c
takeaways: Order: brace, tilde, parameter/arithmetic/command, word splitting, globbing, quote removal
Only unquoted expansion results are split and globbed
"$@" keeps arguments separate; "$*" joins them with the first IFS character
pitfalls: Expecting {1..$n} to produce a range; use seq or a C-style for loop.

quiz.q: Why does `echo {1..$n}` print {1..3} rather than 1 2 3?
options: Brace expansion happens before parameter expansion
quiz.explain: When braces are expanded, $n is still literal text, so the sequence is invalid and left alone.

quiz.q: With IFS=, what does splitting `a,,b` produce?
quiz.explain: Non-whitespace IFS characters delimit exactly, so the empty field between the commas is kept.

concepts.name: How bash runs commands: fork and exec
concepts.summary: Command lookup order, builtins versus programs, fork/exec, $$ versus $BASHPID, lastpipe and exec.
concepts.why: Understanding processes explains performance, why cd must be a builtin and where variables go.
concepts.body:
For a simple command name, bash searches in this order: **aliases** (interactive shells only), **keywords** (`if`, `[[`), **functions**, **builtins**, then the **hash table** of remembered paths and finally the directories in `PATH`. `type -a name` shows every match. `command name` skips functions and aliases; `builtin name` forces the builtin, useful inside a wrapper function of the same name.

An external program runs via **fork** (clone the shell process) then **exec** (replace the clone's image with the program). The parent waits for it unless it was started with `&`. Builtins run inside the shell process, which is why `cd`, `export`, `read` and `source` must be builtins: they change the shell's own state. It is also why a loop that calls an external program thousands of times is slow and one using parameter expansion is fast.

Subshells are forks without exec. `$$` always holds the main shell's PID, while `$BASHPID` gives the current (sub)shell's PID. Bash forks for each pipeline stage; with `shopt -s lastpipe` (non-interactive shells) the last stage runs in the current shell, so `cmd | read -r v` keeps `v`.

`exec cmd` replaces the shell itself, with no fork and no return. Wrapper and container entrypoint scripts end with `exec "$@"` so the real program becomes PID 1 and receives signals directly.
concepts.code:
type -a echo                 # echo is a shell builtin / echo is /usr/bin/echo
echo() { builtin echo "wrapped: $*"; }
echo hi                      # wrapped: hi
command echo hi              # hi   (skips the function)
unset -f echo
echo "main: $$ $BASHPID"     # the same PID twice
( echo "sub:  $$ $BASHPID" ) # $$ unchanged, BASHPID differs
printf 'x\n' | read -r v; echo "v=[$v]"   # v=[]
shopt -s lastpipe            # scripts only: last stage runs here
printf 'x\n' | read -r v; echo "v=[$v]"   # v=[x]
bash -c 'exec echo "replaced"; echo "never printed"'   # replaced
time (for i in {1..200}; do basename /a/b.txt >/dev/null; done)  # slow: 200 forks
time (for i in {1..200}; do : "${p##*/}"; done)                  # fast: no forks
takeaways: Lookup: alias, keyword, function, builtin, hash, PATH
External commands cost a fork and exec; builtins do not
$$ is the main shell, $BASHPID the current subshell; exec replaces the shell
pitfalls: Entrypoint scripts that run the app without exec, leaving the shell as PID 1 that does not forward SIGTERM.

quiz.q: Why must cd be a shell builtin?
options: A child process cannot change its parent's working directory
quiz.explain: An external cd would change only its own process's directory and then exit.

quiz.q: What does a Docker entrypoint script gain by ending with `exec "$@"`?
options: The app replaces the shell and receives signals directly
The script can continue after the app exits
quiz.explain: exec replaces the shell process, so the app becomes PID 1 and gets SIGTERM itself.

concepts.name: File descriptors and exec redirections
concepts.summary: Open, duplicate, swap and close file descriptors, redirect a whole script and use coprocesses.
concepts.why: Advanced logging, locking and two-way communication all rely on managing descriptors yourself.
concepts.body:
Redirections on `exec` without a command apply to the **current shell** for the rest of the script:

- `exec 3> file` opens fd 3 for writing, `exec 3< file` for reading, `exec 3<> file` both,
- `exec 3>&-` closes it,
- `exec {fd}> file` lets bash choose a free number (10 or above) and stores it in `fd`; use `>&"$fd"`.

Duplication `n>&m` makes fd n a copy of fd m **at that moment**, which explains classic tricks. `cmd 2>&1 >/dev/null` sends only stderr into a pipe and discards stdout. `3>&1 1>&2 2>&3 3>&-` swaps stdout and stderr through a spare descriptor.

`exec > >(tee -a run.log) 2>&1` near the top of a script copies all following output to a log file while still showing it. Because the `tee` runs asynchronously, its last lines can appear after the script exits.

Descriptors also power locking: `exec 9> /var/lock/job.lock; flock -n 9 || exit 1` ensures only one instance runs, and the lock is released automatically when the process exits.

`coproc NAME { cmd; }` starts a background process with two pipes; write to `${NAME[1]}` and read from `${NAME[0]}`. Watch for buffering: many programs only flush output when their input closes. Inspect a process's descriptors in `/proc/$$/fd`.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)"
exec 3> log.txt                # fd 3 stays open for the rest of the script
echo "to the log" >&3
exec 3>&-                      # close it
cat log.txt                    # to the log
exec {fd}< /etc/passwd         # bash picks a free fd number
read -r first <&"$fd"; exec {fd}<&-
echo "${first%%:*}"            # root
{ echo out; echo err >&2; } 2>&1 >/dev/null | tr a-z A-Z   # ERR
{ echo out; echo err >&2; } 3>&1 1>&2 2>&3 3>&- | cat   # err via the pipe, out on stderr
exec 9> job.lock
flock -n 9 && echo "got the lock"   # got the lock
coproc UP { tr a-z A-Z; }
echo "hello coproc" >&"${UP[1]}"; exec {UP[1]}>&-
read -r line <&"${UP[0]}"; echo "$line"   # HELLO COPROC
ls /proc/$$/fd                 # 0 1 2 9 255 ...  (open descriptors)
takeaways: exec with only redirections changes the current shell's descriptors
n>&m copies m at that moment; order explains 2>&1 >/dev/null
flock on an fd gives easy single-instance locking
pitfalls: Expecting `cmd >/dev/null 2>&1` and `cmd 2>&1 >/dev/null` to be the same.

quiz.q: What reaches the pipe in `cmd 2>&1 >/dev/null | less`?
quiz.explain: First stderr is pointed at the pipe (current stdout), then stdout is moved to /dev/null.

quiz.q: What does `exec 3>&-` do?
quiz.explain: >&- closes the given descriptor.

concepts.name: POSIX sh, bashisms and when to stop
concepts.summary: Know which features are bash-only, how /bin/sh differs across systems and when a script should become Python.
concepts.why: Scripts run in Alpine containers, on macOS and under dash; knowing the boundaries prevents 'works on my machine'.
concepts.body:
`/bin/sh` is not bash everywhere: it is **dash** on Debian and Ubuntu, BusyBox **ash** in Alpine images and bash in POSIX mode on RHEL. macOS ships an old **bash 3.2** (zsh is its default shell), which lacks associative arrays, `mapfile`, `${var,,}` and `wait -n`. A script with `#!/bin/sh` must stick to POSIX shell.

Common **bashisms** and their POSIX replacements:

- `[[ ]]` becomes `[ ]` with careful quoting, or `case` for patterns,
- arrays become the single list `"$@"` (via `set --`) or newline-separated strings,
- `(( ))` becomes `$(( ))` inside `[ ]`; `function f` becomes `f()`,
- `&>` becomes `> f 2>&1`; `source` becomes `.`; `$'\t'` becomes `printf`,
- `<( )` has no equivalent; use temporary files or FIFOs.

Check portability with `shellcheck --shell=sh`, `checkbashisms`, or simply run the script with `dash`. If you need bash, say so with `#!/usr/bin/env bash` and, if necessary, guard on `BASH_VERSINFO`.

Know when to stop. Shell is excellent for gluing commands together, but once a script passes a couple of hundred lines, manipulates structured data (JSON, CSV with quoting), needs real error handling, floats or unit tests, a language like Python or Go will be shorter and safer. Keep the shell part a thin wrapper.
concepts.code:
# Bash only                          # POSIX sh equivalent
# [[ $x == a* ]] && echo yes        # case $x in a*) echo yes ;; esac
# (( n++ ))                          # n=$((n + 1))
# lower=${s,,}                       # lower=$(printf '%s' "$s" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')
# cmd &> out.log                     # cmd > out.log 2>&1
# source ./lib.sh                    # . ./lib.sh
# arr=(a b c); "${arr[@]}"           # set -- a b c; "$@"
if (( BASH_VERSINFO[0] < 4 )); then  # macOS /bin/bash is 3.2
  echo "this script needs bash >= 4" >&2
  exit 1
fi
printf 'x=1; [[ $x == 1 ]] && echo ok\n' > /tmp/t.sh
bash /tmp/t.sh                       # ok
dash /tmp/t.sh 2>&1 || true          # /tmp/t.sh: 1: [[: not found
takeaways: /bin/sh may be dash, ash or bash in POSIX mode; macOS bash is 3.2
Test portability with shellcheck --shell=sh or by running dash
Move to Python or Go when logic, data or size outgrow the shell
pitfalls: Writing bash features in a script whose shebang is #!/bin/sh: it works on RHEL and fails on Ubuntu.

quiz.q: A #!/bin/sh script using [[ ]] works on Fedora but fails on Ubuntu. Why?
options: Ubuntu's /bin/sh is dash, which has no [[
quiz.explain: On Debian-based systems sh is dash, a strict POSIX shell; on Fedora sh is bash.

quiz.q: Which feature is NOT available in macOS's default /bin/bash 3.2?
quiz.explain: Associative arrays arrived in bash 4.0.
